claim: Direction selectivity in ferret visual cortex develops rapidly over a few days after eye opening.
source: we undertook an intracellular analysis of the development of direction selectivity in the ferret visual cortex, which occurs rapidly over a few days after eye opening.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the developmental timeline.

claim: Strong evidence of developmental changes in linear spatiotemporal receptive fields of simple cells was found.
source: We found strong evidence of developmental changes in linear spatiotemporal receptive fields of simple cells, implying alterations in circuit inputs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Receptive field plasticity was accompanied by increases in near-spike-threshold excitability.
source: Further, this receptive field plasticity was accompanied by increases in near-spike-threshold excitability and input-output gain that resulted in dramatically increased spiking responses in the experienced state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements of spike threshold and excitability.

claim: Receptive field plasticity was accompanied by increases in input-output gain.
source: Further, this receptive field plasticity was accompanied by increases in near-spike-threshold excitability and input-output gain that resulted in dramatically increased spiking responses in the experienced state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-to-firing rate transformation analysis.

claim: Increases in subthreshold membrane responses and increased input-output spiking gain were both necessary to explain elevated firing rates in experienced ferrets.
source: Increases in subthreshold membrane responses induced by the receptive field plasticity and the increased input-output spiking gain were both necessary to explain the elevated firing rates in experienced ferrets.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by modeling simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cortical direction selectivity develops through a combination of plasticity in inputs and in cell-intrinsic properties.
source: These results demonstrate that cortical direction selectivity develops through a combination of plasticity in inputs and in cell-intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract and supported by all experimental findings.

claim: At eye opening in carnivores and primates, neurons exhibit orientation selectivity but respond equally to motion in opposite directions.
source: At the time of eye opening in carnivores and primates, while neurons already exhibit orientation selectivity, they respond about equally to motion in the two opposite directions orthogonal to the preferred axis of orientation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Selectivity to direction of motion develops rapidly in the days and weeks following the onset of visual experience.
source: Selectivity to direction of motion develops rapidly in the days and weeks following the onset of visual experience (Hatta et al., 1998; Li et al., 2006; Clemens et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Direction selectivity can be accelerated in the lab through exposure to moving stimuli.
source: and can be accelerated in the lab through exposure to moving stimuli (Li et al., 2008; Van Hooser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In cats and primates, a set of inputs activating the cell at varying spatial positions and temporal latencies following a specific spatiotemporal order underlies direction selectivity in the visually mature state.
source: In cats and primates, it has been demonstrated that a set of inputs activating the cell at varying spatial positions and temporal latencies following a specific spatiotemporal order underlies direction selectivity in the visually mature state (DeAngelis et al., 1993b; Jagadeesh et al., 1993; McLean et al., 1994; Livingstone, 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the development of the precise pattern of spatiotemporal activation are poorly understood.
source: But the mechanisms underlying the development of this precise pattern of spatiotemporal activation, and consequently of direction selectivity, are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: The contributions of cell-intrinsic properties to the development of direction-selectivity remain largely unexplored.
source: Additionally, the contributions of cell-intrinsic properties to the development of direction-selectivity also remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: In vivo intracellular recordings were carried out in two groups of ferrets: visually naive (P30-34) and visually experienced (P40-60).
source: we carried out in vivo intracellular recordings in V1 from two groups of ferrets at different stages of visual development: visually naive (post-natal day P30-34) and visually experienced (P40-60).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and groups used in the study.

claim: Significant differences in the spatiotemporal organization of receptive fields were found between the visually naive and experienced groups.
source: We found significant differences in the spatiotemporal organization of receptive fields between the visually naive and experienced groups.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: The enhancement in Vm responses brought about by receptive field rearrangements did not successfully predict the developmental enhancement in spiking responses.
source: Surprisingly, the enhancement in Vm responses brought about by these receptive field rearrangements did not successfully predict the developmental enhancement in spiking responses.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the introduction and supported by data comparing Vm and spike responses.

claim: V1 neurons in visually experienced animals had stronger gains in Vm-to-spike transformation.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that V1 neurons in visually experienced animals had stronger gains in Vm-to-spike transformation
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by voltage-to-firing rate analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Gain enhancement was accompanied by a lowering of spike threshold.
source: and that this gain enhancement was accompanied by a lowering of spike threshold.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by spike threshold measurements in Figure 5.

claim: The experienced cells exhibited stronger direction selectivity compared to the naive cells at the subthreshold Vm level.
source: On average, the experienced cells exhibited stronger direction selectivity compared to the naive cells, both at the subthreshold Vm and the suprathreshold spiking levels (Figure 2C, Direction selectivity index or DSI. Top, Vm: naive: mean = 0.16 ± 0.02, n = 23; experienced: mean = 0.35 ± 0.04, n = 29; p<0.001, WRS test
evidence: This is a primary finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: The experienced cells exhibited stronger direction selectivity compared to the naive cells at the suprathreshold spiking level.
source: On average, the experienced cells exhibited stronger direction selectivity compared to the naive cells, both at the subthreshold Vm and the suprathreshold spiking levels (Figure 2C, Direction selectivity index or DSI. Top, Vm: naive: mean = 0.16 ± 0.02, n = 23; experienced: mean = 0.35 ± 0.04, n = 29; p<0.001, WRS test; bottom, spike: naive: mean = 0.3 ± 0.05, n = 14 (9 cells did not spike); experienced: mean = 0.66 ± 0.05, n = 29; p<0.001, WRS test).
evidence: This is a primary finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: In both naive and experienced groups, the spike DSI was significantly higher than Vm DSI.
source: A pairwise comparison of Vm and spike DSI within each neuron revealed that the spike DSI was significantly higher than Vm DSI in both the naive and the experienced groups (Figure 2D; naive, p=0.001, n = 14; experienced, p<0.001, n = 29; signed rank test).
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: In both groups, the outputs of V1 cells were more sharply tuned for direction than their summed inputs.
source: Thus, in both groups, the outputs of V1 cells were more sharply tuned for direction than their summed inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that spike DSI was higher than Vm DSI.

claim: F0 and F1 DSI for both sub- and suprathreshold responses in the experienced group were significantly higher than the naive group.
source: F0 and F1 DSI for both sub- and suprathreshold responses in the experienced group were significantly higher than the naive group (Figure 2E; F0: Vm: naive: mean = 0.15 +/- 0.02, n = 23; experienced: mean = 0.27 +/- 0.04, n = 29; p=0.02, WRS test; spike: naive: mean = 0.33 +/- 0.05, n = 14; experienced: mean = 0.62 +/- 0.05, n = 29; p=0.003, WRS test; F1: Vm: naive: mean = 0.32 +/- 0.04, n = 14; experienced: mean = 0.57 +/- 0.04, n = 29; p<0.001, WRS test; spike: naive: mean = 0.31 +/- 0.06, n = 14; experienced: mean = 0.7 +/- 0.04, n = 29; p<0.001, WRS test)
evidence: This is a primary finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: Both the mean and the modulated component of visual responses became more direction-selective during development.
source: demonstrating that both the mean and the modulated component of visual responses became more direction-selective during development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the F0 and F1 DSI findings.

claim: At the level of Vm, the null responses did not show any significant change over development.
source: At the level of Vm (Figure 2F, top), the null responses (left) did not show any significant change over development, whereas the preferred responses (right) showed a modest but significant increase from the naive to the experienced group (Null, naive: mean = 11 ± 1.2, n = 23; experienced: mean = 11.2 ± 0.9, n = 29, p=0.8, WRS test
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values showing no significant difference.

claim: At the level of Vm, the preferred responses showed a modest but significant increase from the naive to the experienced group.
source: At the level of Vm (Figure 2F, top), the null responses (left) did not show any significant change over development, whereas the preferred responses (right) showed a modest but significant increase from the naive to the experienced group (Null, naive: mean = 11 ± 1.2, n = 23; experienced: mean = 11.2 ± 0.9, n = 29, p=0.8, WRS test; Preferred, naive: mean = 13.1 ± 1.3, n = 23; experienced: mean = 17.3 ± 0.9, n = 29, p=0.008, WRS test).
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: At the level of spiking, both the null and the preferred responses underwent developmental enhancement.
source: At the level of spiking (Figure 2F, bottom), both the null and the preferred responses underwent developmental enhancement (null, naive: mean = 4.8 ± 1.2, n = 23; experienced: mean = 9 ± 1.5, n = 29, p=0.01, WRS test; preferred, naive: mean = 6.6 ± 1.6, n = 23; experienced: mean = 24.7 ± 2.6, n = 29, p<0.001, WRS test).
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: The increase in direction selectivity following visual experience was driven primarily by a robust increase in responses to the preferred direction of motion and not by a decrease in response to the null direction of motion.
source: Therefore, the increase in direction selectivity following visual experience was driven primarily by a robust increase in responses to the preferred direction of motion and not by a decrease in response to the null direction of motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the preferred and null response data.

claim: While the increase in response to the preferred direction was modest (32%) at the Vm level, it was dramatic for spiking activity (274%).
source: Notably, while this increase in response to the preferred direction was modest (32%) at the Vm level, it was dramatic for spiking activity (274%).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the magnitude of changes at different levels.

claim: The spatiotemporal receptive field subunits from direction-selective neurons in experienced animals were slanted in space-time.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Reid et al., 1987; Reid et al., 1991; DeAngelis et al., 1993b; Priebe and Ferster, 2005), the spatiotemporal receptive field subunits from direction-selective neurons in experienced animals were slanted in space-time.
evidence: This is a finding consistent with prior literature, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The subunits from the experienced cells were longer and narrower in profile, and relatively more slanted in space-time compared to naive cells.
source: However, the subunits from the experienced cells were longer and narrower in profile, and relatively more slanted in space-time.
evidence: This is a qualitative description of differences observed in the receptive field data.

claim: Six out of nine receptive field shape parameters were significantly different between the naive and the experienced groups: eccentricity, major axis, minor axis, orientation, temporal extent and minimum latency.
source: Wilcoxon rank sum test comparisons revealed that six out of these nine parameters were significantly different between the naive and the experienced groups: eccentricity, major axis, minor axis, orientation, temporal extent and minimum latency.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparisons of receptive field parameters.

claim: The eccentricity measured from the experienced subunits were significantly higher.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that the eccentricity measured from the experienced subunits were significantly higher (p<0.001), and was caused by both a longer major axis (p<0.03) and a shorter minor axis (p<0.03, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical significance values.

claim: The subunits from the experienced animals subtended a smaller angle on the space axis.
source: Also, the subunits from the experienced animals subtended a smaller angle on the space axis (orientation: p<0.005), which would indicate that the cells from experienced animals are tuned to higher motion velocities, consistent with data from actual V1 recordings in cats (DeAngelis et al., 1993a).
evidence: This is a finding with statistical significance and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The overall area and the spatial projection of the subunits did not significantly differ between naive and experienced groups.
source: The overall area (p<0.6) and the spatial projection (p<0.35) of the subunits did not significantly differ.
evidence: This is a finding showing no significant difference for these parameters.

claim: The projection on the latency axis was significantly longer in the experienced group.
source: However, the projection on the latency axis was significantly longer in the experienced group (p<0.04), suggesting that a longer range of response latencies became available in the experienced animals.
evidence: This is a finding with statistical significance and interpretation.

claim: The extension of the latency range was achieved solely by stretching the receptive field subunits towards the lower latency side.
source: This extension of the latency range was achieved solely by stretching the receptive field subunits towards the lower latency side: while the maximum latencies of the subunits were not significantly different (p<0.3), the minimum latencies were significantly lower in the experienced group (p<0.05).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the latency data with statistical support.

claim: The Vm response latency distributions were significantly shifted towards shorter latencies in the experienced animals.
source: Consistent with this data, we also found that the Vm response latency distributions were significantly shifted towards shorter latencies in the experienced animals (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Reduced latencies observed in experienced vs. naive neurons mirror those in ferret lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: and these results mirror reduced latencies observed in experienced vs. naive neurons in ferret lateral geniculate nucleus (Tavazoie and Reid, 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature findings.

claim: The Vm direction index of the cells increased with increasing 'narrowness' of the subunits (longer 'major axis', shorter 'minor axis' and higher 'eccentricity').
source: We found that the Vm direction index of the cells increased with increasing 'narrowness' of the subunits (longer 'major axis', shorter 'minor axis' and higher 'eccentricity'), 'orientation', if the one low outlier is removed, and decreasing minimum latencies accessible (lower 'min latency').
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Vm DSI predicted from the STRFs showed a linear correlation with the actually measured Vm DSI of the F1 components of the simple cells.
source: Additionally, the Vm DSI predicted from the STRFs, by converting the STRFs into the frequency domain via 2-dimensional FFT, showed a linear correlation with the actually measured Vm DSI of the F1 components of the simple cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Following visual experience, the Vm receptive fields exhibited marked reorganization involving increased eccentricity of the space-time profile and a shift of response latencies towards lower values.
source: In sum, following visual experience, the Vm receptive fields exhibited marked reorganization involving increased eccentricity of the space-time profile and a shift of response latencies towards lower values, leading to improved discrimination of directional inputs at subthreshold level and thus a more direction-selective Vm response.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the receptive field findings.

claim: The fraction of cells that fired action potentials in response to drifting grating stimuli was significantly higher in the experienced group.
source: The fraction of cells that fired action potentials in response to drifting grating stimuli was significantly higher in the experienced group (simple: naive, 7/10; experienced, 16/16; p<0.05, complex: naive, 7/13; experienced, 13/13; p<0.05, Fisher Exact test).
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: Every recorded cell in the experienced group fired action potentials, but 9/23 cells in the naive group did not fire any action potentials at all.
source: Thus, every recorded cell in the experienced group fired action potentials, but 9/23 cells in the naive group did not fire any action potentials at all.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data.

claim: Enhancement of Vm responses mediated by reorganization of STRF structure alone could not account for enhanced spiking.
source: However, enhancement of Vm responses mediated by reorganization of STRF structure alone could not account for this enhanced spiking.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the discrepancy between Vm and spike response changes.

claim: In the naive group, the spikes were significantly broader than in the experienced group.
source: Visual inspection of spike waveforms revealed a couple of striking differences between the naive and the experienced groups: in the naive group, the spikes were significantly broader and the take-off point of the action potential (spike threshold) was higher (Figure 5ABC).
evidence: This is a finding from visual inspection and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The take-off point of the action potential (spike threshold) was higher in the naive group than in the experienced group.
source: Visual inspection of spike waveforms revealed a couple of striking differences between the naive and the experienced groups: in the naive group, the spikes were significantly broader and the take-off point of the action potential (spike threshold) was higher (Figure 5ABC).
evidence: This is a finding from visual inspection and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In vivo, the maximum dV/dt exhibited a strong increase between naive and experienced animals.
source: In vivo, the maximum dV/dt exhibited a strong increase between naive and experienced animals (Figure 5C, naive mean: 172.2 ± 64.6 mV/ms, experienced mean: 253 ± 78.3 mV/ms, WRS test p<2.0e-04)
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: In vivo, there was a small empirical drop in spike kink voltage that was not statistically significant.
source: a small empirical drop in spike kink voltage (Figure 5D, naive mean: 21 ± 0.4 mV, experienced mean: 19.1 ± 4.7 mV, WRS test p=0.21, not statistically significant)
evidence: This is a finding showing no significant difference.

claim: In vivo, there was a very substantial decrease in action potential width between naive and experienced animals.
source: and a very substantial decrease in action potential width (Figure 5E, naive mean: 1.6 ± 0.7 ms, experienced mean: 1.0 ± 0.4 msec, WRS test p<4.3e-04).
evidence: This is a finding with specific statistical values and significance testing.

claim: Maximum dV/dt measurements in slice strongly resembled those measured in vivo.
source: Maximum dV/dt measurements in slice (Figure 5F) strongly resembled those measured in vivo (naive mean: 162.1 ± 51.1 mV/ms, experienced mean: 264.4 ± 61.9 mV/ms, WRS n vs. e, p<2.4e-05).
evidence: This is a finding comparing in vivo and ex vivo measurements.

claim: The spike kink voltage exhibited a small, significant decrease with experience in slice measurements.
source: The spike kink voltage exhibited a small, significant decrease with experience (naive mean: −25 ± 3.5 mV, experienced mean: −30.2 ± 3.7 mV), consistent with the idea that the experienced cells were more excitable near threshold.
evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo measurements with interpretation.

claim: Input resistance exhibited a drop with developmental age.
source: As expected for developing animals, input resistance exhibited a drop with developmental age (naive mean: 222.9 ± 57.9 MΩ, experienced mean: 144.8 ± 39.3 MΩ)
evidence: This is a finding consistent with developmental expectations.

claim: The firing rate vs. input current curves (F-I curves) were not different across the two groups.
source: The firing rate vs. input current curves (F-I curves) were not different across the two groups (Figure 5IJK; f-I curve Kruskal-Wallis test of linear slopes: p<0.068).
evidence: This is a finding showing no significant difference.

claim: On average, experienced cells exhibited significantly higher firing rates than naive cells over a wide range of voltages.
source: Generally, most naive cells exhibited smaller firing rates for a given voltage than the experienced cells, which reflects the increased excitability of the mature neurons. On average, experienced cells exhibited significantly higher firing rates than naive cells over a wide range of voltages (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from voltage-to-firing rate analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The phenomenological model did an excellent job of reproducing the actual firing rates recorded for each stimulus and each cell for both naive and experienced cells.
source: This phenomenological model did an excellent job of reproducing the actual firing rates recorded for each stimulus and each cell for both naive and experienced cells (Figure 7AB).
evidence: This is a finding from model validation shown in Figure 7AB.

claim: Changes in the underlying selectivity of the voltage waveforms from naive to experienced was sufficient to confer increased direction selectivity values.
source: Therefore, changes in the underlying selectivity of the voltage waveforms from naive to experienced was sufficient to confer increased direction selectivity values across these conditions, but the increased gain of the experienced voltage-to-firing rate transforms were needed to also confer the higher firing rates observed in experienced animals (Figure 7CDEF).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the bootstrap simulation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The increased gain of the experienced voltage-to-firing rate transforms were needed to confer the higher firing rates observed in experienced animals.
source: Therefore, changes in the underlying selectivity of the voltage waveforms from naive to experienced was sufficient to confer increased direction selectivity values across these conditions, but the increased gain of the experienced voltage-to-firing rate transforms were needed to also confer the higher firing rates observed in experienced animals (Figure 7CDEF).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the bootstrap simulation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mature receptive fields became elongated along the temporal axis, particularly by exhibiting responses with shorter response latencies that did not exist in the naive state.
source: On the one hand, the mature receptive fields became elongated along the temporal axis, particularly by exhibiting responses with shorter response latencies that did not exist in the naive state.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the receptive field findings in the Discussion.

claim: The mature receptive fields also became significantly narrow in space-time, providing evidence for a narrowing process.
source: However, the mature receptive fields also became significantly narrow in space-time, providing evidence for a narrowing process.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the receptive field findings in the Discussion.

claim: At eye opening, neurons in vivo exhibit weak spiking activity.
source: At eye opening, neurons in vivo exhibit weak spiking activity (Clemens et al., 2012) (this study)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation and current study.

claim: Both rats and ferrets exhibit wide action potentials at eye opening.
source: and both rats (Kasper et al., 1994) and ferrets (this study) exhibit wide action potentials.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation and current study.

claim: As neurons are maturing during this stage just after eye opening, their input resistance rapidly decreases.
source: Further, as neurons are maturing during this stage just after eye opening, their input resistance also rapidly decreases (Kasper et al., 1994; Desai et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies in rats have shown that layer 4 neurons add synapses during this time.
source: Previous studies in rats have shown that layer 4 neurons add synapses during this time (Desai et al., 2002)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Spike threshold decreases during early visual development.
source: and that spike threshold decreases (Kasper et al., 1994), presumably to bring the visual response rates up to mature values and to overcome the decreasing input resistance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation with interpretation.

claim: The weight of feed-forward connections increases substantially at the retinogeniculate synapse (~50 fold over the first week of vision).
source: In other feed-forward systems, the weight of feed-forward connections increases substantially: ~50 fold over the first week of vision at the retinogeniculate synapse (Chen and Regehr, 2000)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The weight of feed-forward connections increases 2–4 fold from P4 to P15 in the barrel cortex.
source: and 2–4 fold from P4 to P15 in the barrel cortex (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Feed-forward synaptic contributions to visual cortex are likely to be increasing during development.
source: Because subthreshold voltage responses increase over the first week of vision and because input resistance is going down, feed-forward synaptic contributions to visual cortex are also likely to be increasing, although we are not aware of direct measurements that would confirm this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the data and lack of direct measurements.

claim: Increases in sodium channel density at the axon initial segment may underlie the enhancement in the maximum slope of Vm during an action potential (max dV/dt) and decreased threshold.
source: Increases in sodium channel density at the axon initial segment may underlie the enhancement in the maximum slope of Vm during an action potential (max dV/dt) and decreased threshold observed here (Colbert and Pan, 2002; Kole et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2009; Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Kuba et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The spike threshold non-linearity contributes substantially to cortical direction selectivity.
source: The spike threshold non-linearity contributes substantially to cortical direction selectivity (Reid et al., 1987; Jagadeesh et al., 1993; Priebe et al., 2004; Priebe and Ferster, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Increased input-output gain did not, by itself, account for the increased direction selectivity index values.
source: The experiments here show that increased input-output gain does contribute to the increased firing rates that are observed in experienced animals, but that increased input-output gain did not, by itself, account for the increased direction selectivity index values (see Figure 7CD).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Changes in the underlying voltage responses were necessary to confer increased direction selectivity.
source: Instead, changes in the underlying voltage responses were necessary to confer increased direction selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: The number of excitatory synapses being formed in ferret and human visual cortex during this time are greatly increasing.
source: These results fit nicely with prior anatomical observations that the number of excitatory synapses being formed in ferret and human visual cortex during this time are greatly increasing (Huttenlocher, 1990; Durack and Katz, 1996; Ruthazer and Stryker, 1996; White et al., 2001; Erisir and Harris, 2003; White and Fitzpatrick, 2007)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: LGN neuron latency drops during the first weeks of visual experience.
source: For example, LGN neuron latency drops during the first weeks of visual experience Tavazoie and Reid, 2000
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There is clear evidence linking the spatiotemporal structure of LGN inputs to direction selectivity in V1 in mice and carnivores.
source: Regardless of whether LGN inputs are altered or constant, there is clear evidence linking the spatiotemporal structure of LGN inputs to direction selectivity in V1 in mice and carnivores (Kremkow et al., 2016; Lien and Scanziani, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Only female ferrets were used because housing mature male and female ferrets in the same room causes significant hormonal stress for the female animals if they are not allowed to mate.
source: Only female ferrets were used because housing mature male and female ferrets in the same room causes significant hormonal stress for the female animals if they are not allowed to mate.
evidence: This is a methodological justification based on animal welfare considerations.

claim: Cells were classified as simple or complex by comparing the fundamental (F1) and the DC components (F0) of the visual responses.
source: Cells were classified as simple or complex by comparing the fundamental (F1) and the DC components (F0) of the visual responses (Carandini and Ferster, 2000; Mechler and Ringach, 2002; Priebe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citations.

claim: Cells with spike modulation ratio equal to or greater than 1.0 were classified as simple, while the rest were categorized as complex.
source: Cells with spike modulation ratio equal to or greater than 1.0 were classified as simple, while the rest were categorized as complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description of cell classification criteria.

claim: The dataset contained 10 simple and 13 complex cells in the naive group, and 16 simple and 13 complex cells in the experienced group.
source: According to this classification, our dataset contained 10 simple and 13 complex cells in the naive group, and 16 simple and 13 complex cells in the experienced group.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset composition.
